recommendation: Keep building off steep slopes, and keep the slopes wooded
what_was_done: Since 2016, rural subdivision rules protect slopes over 15% when land is subdivided in rural policy areas. Countywide, residential grading limits still start at 20%, lots of an acre or more are exempt, and the 15% rule NashvilleNext asked Metro to begin work on within 1 to 3 years (2015) has not been enacted.
evidence: RECOMMENDATIONS-IMPLEMENTATION.md P01; Subdivision Regulations Ch. 4; BL2022-1121; pair 21

recommendation: Preserve the Highland Rim escarpment as a natural landscape
what_was_done: Rural and Conservation policy and the 2016 rural subdivision rules cover much of the Rim, but the policies "are not regulatory" and the Rim has never been mapped or protected by name. In 2025 Council recognized it as "Nashville's Highland Rim Forest" (recognition only; no boundary, rules or funding); a Highland Rim Forests master plan has been in the capital budget since 2024, "Not started."

recommendation: Keep sewers and urban services out of rural Rim land
what_was_done: The rural no-sewer policy is applied when land is rezoned (Cato Road upzonings denied 2022 and 2023), but Metro Water decides sewer extensions on capacity and developer funding with no rural-policy check, and Council keeps accepting new sewer mains in the Whites Creek corridor. The Alliance reports an extension under way to the Best Brands warehouse; records requested.

recommendation: Keep rural land rural and low density
what_was_done: Rural policy is applied through 2016 rural subdivision rules, downzonings and denied upzonings, but binding tools stop at subdivision, and the recommended agricultural zoning category was never created.

recommendation: Require conservation subdivisions that keep open space
what_was_done: Recommended by right with 50% open space (2011, 2015); a 2006 bill was withdrawn. The 2022 Conservation Development rule keeps 20%, is mandatory only in R and RS zones, and does not reach AR2a or AG land.

recommendation: Protect existing trees on private land during development
what_was_done: 2022 tree rules protect retained trees and require replacement once land is under development review, but nothing requires keeping existing trees; the 2022 canopy retention bill was withdrawn in 2023.

recommendation: Hold the county's tree canopy, including large forested tracts
what_was_done: Canopy grew 5,247 acres 2010-2021 but fell about 900 acres 2016-2021, all in the urban district; rural canopy grew and is above its goal. Planting is funded, but no rule protects large forested tracts on private land.
evidence: P07; Urban Tree Canopy Assessment 2023; BL2021-972

recommendation: Buy and protect natural land on and around the Rim
what_was_done: Metro buys Rim land when chances arise (Beaman Park 2015; about 300 acres announced in 2026, transfer pending closing; easements 2009) but has no acquisition program or land bank. Metro reports $12.8 million allocated for park land since 2017, against a 2017 estimated market value of $534 million for recommended land; the two are different measures. A $7 million Highland Rim conservation easement project is listed in the adopted FY2027 capital budget (27DS0031, $7,000,000, requested by At-Large CM Burkley Allen; adopted CIB p III-91); FY2027 Capital Spending Plan not yet issued as of 2026-11-02.
evidence: P08; RS2025-1556; FY2027 CIB 27DS0031; pairs 2, 14, 18, 25; FY26 Report on Council Requests 26-01-02 (CM Kimbrough, Conservation Assistance Fund; Planning: recommend not including, p6); FY27 Report on Council Requests 27-39-02 (CM Allen, p369); FY27 Council CIB Prioritization Report (rank 12 of 187)

what_was_done: Parkland grew (about 11,000 acres in 2011 to 15,657 in 2025 on Metro figures, which conflict), but Plan to Play's 4,541-acre target for 2026 is not yet due (568.78 acres reported; about 300 acres next to Beaman Park pending closing), and the 22,000-acre, private, regulatory and agricultural goals were never reported against.

recommendation: Keep the Open Space Fund replenished
what_was_done: No record found in FY2017 to FY2026 Capital Spending Plans names the Open Space Fund or its balance (searched 2026-11-02: every Capital Spending Plan file on the Finance capital budget page, FY2018 to FY2026 exhibits, resolutions, memos and presentation, and the Plan to Play 2026 Appendix; FY2017 has no spending plan file on that page); land money arrives in irregular capital allocations, zero in most years.
evidence: P10; pair 19; absence check 2026-11-02 (FY2018 to FY2026 Capital Spending Plan files, Plan to Play 2026 Appendix)

recommendation: Use conservation easements and transfer of development rights
what_was_done: Metro used easements once (290 acres, 2009) and has a 2017 grant fund that can pay for them, but no grants were found, the FY2027 Highland Rim conservation easement project is listed in the adopted FY2027 capital budget (27DS0031, $7,000,000, requested by At-Large CM Burkley Allen; adopted CIB p III-91); FY2027 Capital Spending Plan not yet issued as of 2026-11-02, and no transfer of development rights exists for natural land.
evidence: P11; RS2009-941; BL2017-725; FY2027 CIB 27DS0031; FY26 Report on Council Requests 26-01-02 (CM Kimbrough, Conservation Assistance Fund; Planning: recommend not including, p6); FY27 Report on Council Requests 27-39-02 (CM Allen, p369)

recommendation: Join regional efforts to conserve upstream land
what_was_done: No Metro agreement or program for upstream or regional land conservation was found. The 2015 action names regional partners as implementers, not a Metro department.

recommendation: Designate and actively manage Metro's natural areas
what_was_done: The Park Board adopted a Designated Natural Areas policy on August 4, 2026, with the first 14 sites on its September agenda; site management plans, a target share and a Council ordinance do not exist yet.

recommendation: Run a funded urban forestry program and keep canopy studies current
what_was_done: Urban forestry staff and five-year canopy studies are in the Metro Code (2021), and a dedicated tree fund of up to $2.5 million a year is permanent (2026).

recommendation: Protect rare habitats and species (cedar glades, wetlands, aquatic habitat, invasive pests)
what_was_done: Stream buffers have protected aquatic habitat since the late 1990s; no Metro rule was found for the habitat overlay, wetland mitigation, cedar glades or invasive species asked for.

recommendation: Protect scenic hills, vistas and roadside corridors
what_was_done: About 120 miles of roads are tagged Scenic, with scenic easements required when land along them is subdivided; scenic hills and vistas were never identified or protected.
evidence: P16; Major and Collector Street Plan; Subdivision Regulations 3-10.5

recommendation: Site development around existing trees, land forms and natural features
what_was_done: Tree surveys and root-zone protection are binding, but compliance is measured by replacement density, and site-design guidance is not regulatory.

recommendation: Assemble a connected system of protected natural areas and open space
what_was_done: Land is added piece by piece and a $1.01 million Ecological Conservation Strategy is under way, but there is no adopted, mapped system of protected natural areas.

recommendation: Broad goals to protect and invest in the natural environment
what_was_done: The goals have no measurable target; NashvilleNext progress reports stop after 2016, and the climate plan's green-space baseline is due in FY2027.
